source.title: Adversarial Decoding: Generating Readable Documents for Adversarial Objectives
source.authors: Collin Zhang; Tingwei Zhang; Vitaly Shmatikov

record.file_problem: No apparent truncation or garbling; the paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether adversarial suffix-based inputs can elicit harmful responses from safety-trained instruct models, using attack success rates rather than the original fine-tuning or token-position analyses.
record.gate_note: The paper directly tests jailbreak attacks and reports harmful-response rates, so these are recorded for V4. Fine-tuning safety erosion, per-token KL concentration, localized safety parameters, causes of shallowness, and safety-deepening training are not tested. The RAG poisoning and readability results do not test the listed claim versions. Table 6 values attributed to prior work are not included; only the paper’s own AdvDec and BEAST results are recorded. Llama Guard safe-classification rates are included as findings that do not measure harmful completion rates.
record.test_reason: The paper reports HarmBench harmful-response rates for safety-trained instruct models under readable adversarial suffixes. Each suffix is appended to a short template asking the model to open compliantly ('Please first say "Sure, ..."'). This bears directly on V4, whether a compliant opening plus suffixes defeats refusal. Jailbreaking is only an illustration of the attack method, and no no-attack baseline is reported.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that adversarial decoding produces readable documents effective for RAG poisoning, jailbreaking and Llama Guard evasion. Its success rates are competitive with methods that produce unreadable text, and perplexity and readability filters do not catch its output. They describe the combined evasion-plus-jailbreak result (30% overall) as the first such attack. They use jailbreaking 'solely to illustrate' the method and draw no conclusions about how deep safety alignment goes.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses adversarial decoding to generate suffix attacks and evaluates harmful responses; it does not fine-tune models or measure token-position KL. The authors provide code at https://github.com/collinzrj/adversarial_decoding.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack success differs by model and by objective setup (combined, guard-only, or jailbreak-only).

fits_no_version.finding: AdvDec and BEAST suffixes make Llama-Guard-3-8B classify harmful inputs as safe at 70-95%. Combined with target jailbreak, overall success is 30% (AdvDec) and 35% (BEAST).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Readable adversarial suffixes can evade a guard classifier while still eliciting harmful output, with trade-offs between the two objectives.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference of the European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The reported evaluations provide no uncertainty estimates. Table 7 reports results on HarmBench but does not provide per-item or seed-level variation. Table 6 contains baseline values from prior work that are not recorded here; the authors' own BEAST measurements are limited to Llama and Qwen.
record.rows_left_out: No other results relevant to the listed versions were left out. RAG poisoning, readability-filter, and unrelated benchmark results are outside these versions.

untested.parts: All of it; no fine-tuning is done.
All of it; there is no per-token KL or position analysis.
The following are not tested: literal prefilling of the response, decoding-parameter changes, the template alone without a suffix, and no-attack baseline rates.

missing.what: No baseline harmful-response rate without any attack, and none for the template alone without a suffix. A researcher cannot separate the effect of the compliant-opening request from the suffix.

record.verdict_notes: This is primarily an attack-method paper. The V4-relevant evidence is incidental: a template asking the model to open with 'Sure, I'll...' plus a suffix achieves about 65-73% HarmBench ASR. Vicuna is only weakly safety-trained. Table 6 baseline values (GCG, AutoDAN, COLD, PAIR, and BEAST on Vicuna) come from prior work and are correctly excluded. No uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: Whether harmful fine-tuning examples make a safety-trained model comply.
Whether benign fine-tuning data raises harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.
Tests adversarial suffix and prompt-template attacks, but not literal compliant-token prefilling or decoding changes.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behavior.
Whether training data or objectives cause safety shallowness.
Whether safety-deepening training works or remains robust.

statements.correction: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct jailbreak ASR: AdvDec 73.5% jailbreak-only, 35.0% combined; BEAST 64.5% jailbreak-only, 45.0% combined. Combined-objective verdict: limits_scope. BEAST compliant-opening template: not stated.
statements.problem: The ASRs and objective dependence are correct, but the challenges label overstates this study: harmful-response success remains substantial under the combined objective.
